# What is AI?

## A simple definition

**AI** means **Artificial Intelligence**. *Artificial* means made by humans. *Intelligence* means the ability to learn, understand and solve problems.

So AI is a computer program that can do things which normally need human intelligence. For example:

- Understanding your voice when you say "Ok Google".
- Finding your friend's face in a photo.
- Suggesting the next video on YouTube.
- Finding the fastest route from Gajuwaka to RK Beach on Google Maps.
- Writing an email when you give it a few words.

A normal program follows fixed rules written by a programmer. An AI program **learns** from examples. This is the big difference.

## A short background

AI is not new. Here is a very short history.

- **1950:** Alan Turing asked, "Can machines think?" He suggested a test. If a machine can chat like a human, we can call it intelligent.
- **1956:** The name "Artificial Intelligence" was used for the first time at a meeting in Dartmouth, USA.
- **1960s to 1980s:** Early AI used rules written by experts. It worked for small problems. It failed for big ones. People lost interest. This time is called the "AI winter".
- **1997:** IBM's Deep Blue computer beat the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov.
- **2012:** A new method called **deep learning** became very good at seeing images. AI started to grow fast.
- **2017:** Google researchers made the **Transformer**. This is the design used by ChatGPT and Gemini today.
- **2022:** ChatGPT was released. In two months, 100 million people used it. This started the Generative AI wave.
- **Today:** AI can write, draw, talk, code and even make videos.

## Three kinds of AI

| Kind | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Narrow AI | Does one job well | Google Maps, spam filter, face unlock |
| Generative AI | Creates new text, images, audio or code | ChatGPT, Gemini |
| General AI (AGI) | Can do any task a human can do | Does not exist yet |

All the AI we use today is narrow AI or generative AI. AGI is still a dream.

## Why should an engineer learn AI tools?

You will use AI tools in every branch. A civil engineer can ask AI to check a report. A mechanical engineer can ask AI to write a Python script to read sensor data. A chemical engineer can ask AI to explain a reaction. AI tools are like a calculator. They do not replace you. They make you faster.

> Think of AI as a smart helper. It is fast and knows many things. But it can make mistakes. You are the engineer. You must check its work.

## Try it

- Open [chatgpt.com](https://chatgpt.com) or [gemini.google.com](https://gemini.google.com). Type: *"Explain AI to a first year engineering student in Visakhapatnam in 5 simple sentences."*
- Ask the same tool: *"Give 5 examples of AI that I use every day on my phone."*
- Watch this short video: [What is AI? – CrashCourse](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a0_lo_GDcFw).

## New words

- **Artificial** — made by humans, not natural.
- **Intelligence** — the ability to learn, understand and solve problems.
- **Program** — a set of instructions that a computer follows.
- **Rule** — a fixed instruction like "if X then do Y".
- **Deep learning** — a way for computers to learn from a lot of examples, using many layers of maths.
- **Transformer** — the design (architecture) used inside ChatGPT and Gemini.
- **Narrow AI** — AI that does only one kind of job.
- **AGI** — Artificial General Intelligence; an AI that can do anything a human can. Not real yet.

# How AI learns

## Data, model, prediction

Most AI today works in three steps.

1. **Data.** We collect many examples. For example, 10,000 photos of cats and 10,000 photos of dogs.
2. **Training.** The computer looks at the examples again and again. It slowly adjusts numbers inside itself until it gets most answers right. The result is called a **model**.
3. **Prediction.** We give the model a new photo. It says "cat" or "dog". This is called a prediction, or an **output**.

The whole method is called **Machine Learning (ML)**. The machine learns from data. Nobody writes the rules by hand.

## A small example

Suppose you want to predict the price of a flat in Madhurawada. You collect data: size of the flat, floor, distance from the beach and the price. You give this data to an ML model. It learns the pattern. Then you give it a new flat. It predicts the price.

The model is not magic. It only finds patterns in the data you gave it. If your data is bad, the model is bad. There is a saying: **garbage in, garbage out**.

## Three ways of learning

| Way | How it works | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Supervised learning | Data has the correct answers (labels) | Photos labelled "cat" or "dog" |
| Unsupervised learning | Data has no labels; the model finds groups | Grouping customers by what they buy |
| Reinforcement learning | The model gets a reward when it does well | A game-playing AI, a robot learning to walk |

## Neural networks

A **neural network** is a type of model. It is loosely inspired by the brain. It has many small units called **neurons**, arranged in **layers**. Each neuron does a small calculation. Together, millions of them can learn very complex patterns.

When a network has many layers, we call it **deep learning**. Deep learning is behind almost all modern AI: voice assistants, face unlock, self-driving cars and ChatGPT.

## Training needs a lot of power

Training a big model needs:

- A lot of data (the whole internet, in some cases).
- A lot of computers with special chips called **GPUs**.
- A lot of electricity and money.

This is why only big companies like Google, OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic train the largest models. But anyone can **use** them. That is what this course is about.

## Try it

- Play [Quick, Draw!](https://quickdraw.withgoogle.com/) by Google. You draw. The AI guesses. Every drawing becomes training data.
- Try [Teachable Machine](https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/). Train your own image model in 5 minutes using your webcam. No code needed.
- Ask Gemini: *"Explain supervised learning with an example from a Vizag fish market."*

## New words

- **Data** — facts, numbers, text or images that a computer can store.
- **Model** — the result of training; the "brain" that gives predictions.
- **Training** — the process of learning from data.
- **Prediction** — the answer a model gives for a new input.
- **Label** — the correct answer attached to a piece of data.
- **Pattern** — something that repeats in data.
- **Neural network** — a model made of many small connected units (neurons).
- **Layer** — a group of neurons in a network.
- **GPU** — Graphics Processing Unit; a chip that is very fast at the maths AI needs.

# Generative AI and LLMs

## What is Generative AI?

Old AI mainly **classified** things. Is this a cat or a dog? Is this email spam or not?

**Generative AI** is different. It **creates** new things. It can write a poem, draw a picture, compose music, make a video or write a program. The word *generate* means *to make*.

| Input you give | Generative AI makes |
|---|---|
| "Write a poem about Rushikonda beach" | A new poem |
| "A fishing boat at sunrise, oil painting" | A new image |
| "Write a C program to add two numbers" | New code |
| A 20-page PDF | A short summary |

## What is an LLM?

An **LLM** is a **Large Language Model**. It is the engine inside ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude.

- **Large** — it has billions of numbers (called parameters) inside it.
- **Language** — it works with text: English, Telugu, Hindi, Python, C and more.
- **Model** — it was trained on a huge amount of text from books and the internet.

## How does an LLM work? (Simple version)

An LLM does one thing. It guesses the **next word**.

Give it "Visakhapatnam is a city on the east". It guesses "coast". Add that and ask again. It guesses "of". Then "India". It keeps going, one word at a time, until the answer is complete.

That is all. But because it read so much text, its guesses are very good. It can answer questions, write essays and write code just by guessing the next word again and again.

> Actually, the model works with **tokens**, not words. A token is a word or a part of a word. "Visakhapatnam" might be 4 tokens. You will see the word *token* in many AI tools.

## Important things to know about LLMs

1. **They can be wrong.** An LLM does not "know" facts. It guesses what sounds right. Sometimes it makes up things that are false. This is called a **hallucination**. Always check important facts.
2. **They have a cut-off date.** The model learned from text up to some date. It may not know last month's news. Some tools fix this by searching the web.
3. **They have a context window.** This is how much text the model can read at one time. If you paste a very long document, the model may forget the start.
4. **They are not alive.** An LLM has no feelings, no opinions and no memory of you (unless the app saves your chat).
5. **Same question, different answers.** LLMs use a little randomness. Ask twice and you may get two different answers.

## Other generative models

- **Image models** make pictures from text. Examples: Imagen (Google), DALL·E and GPT Image (OpenAI), Midjourney, Stable Diffusion.
- **Audio models** make speech or music. Examples: ElevenLabs, Suno.
- **Video models** make short videos. Examples: Veo (Google), Sora (OpenAI).
- **Multimodal models** can handle text, images, audio and video together. Gemini and GPT are multimodal. You can show them a photo and ask a question about it.

## Try it

- In Gemini or ChatGPT, type only: *"Visakhapatnam is a city on the"* and see how it continues the sentence.
- Upload a photo of your handwritten notes to Gemini and ask it to type them out.
- See how text becomes tokens: [OpenAI Tokenizer](https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer). Type your name and a Telugu word.
- Short video: [How LLMs work – 3Blue1Brown](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LPZh9BOjkQs).

## New words

- **Generate** — to make or create something new.
- **Classify** — to put something into a group (cat or dog, spam or not spam).
- **LLM** — Large Language Model; an AI trained on a huge amount of text.
- **Parameter** — a number inside a model that was set during training.
- **Token** — a word or part of a word; the unit an LLM reads and writes.
- **Hallucination** — when an AI confidently gives a wrong or made-up answer.
- **Cut-off date** — the last date of the data the model was trained on.
- **Context window** — the amount of text a model can look at in one go.
- **Multimodal** — can work with many types of input: text, image, audio, video.

# Where Generative AI is used

Generative AI is already used in many fields. Here are the main ones. Think about which ones matter for your branch.

## Education

- Explaining a hard topic in simple words, in English or Telugu.
- Making practice questions before an exam.
- Summarising a long chapter into one page.
- Acting as a patient tutor at 2 am.

## Writing and office work

- Writing emails, letters, notices and reports.
- Fixing grammar and spelling.
- Translating between languages.
- Making slides for a presentation.

## Software and engineering

- Writing code in C, Python, Java and more.
- Finding and fixing bugs.
- Writing test cases and documentation.
- Explaining old code that someone else wrote.

## Design and media

- Making images, logos and posters from text.
- Making greeting cards and social media posts.
- Generating voice-overs and background music.
- Making short videos.

## Healthcare

- Writing a summary of a patient's history for a doctor.
- Helping to read X-rays and scans (with a doctor checking).
- Answering common health questions in local languages.

## Agriculture

- A farmer in Anakapalle can take a photo of a sick plant and ask what is wrong.
- Advice on weather, crops and prices in Telugu.
- Government schemes explained in simple words.

## Business and marketing

- Writing product descriptions and advertisements.
- Chatbots that answer customer questions 24 hours a day.
- Studying customer reviews to find common complaints.

## Science and research

- Reading hundreds of research papers and giving a summary.
- Suggesting new molecules for medicines.
- Helping to write and check research papers.

## Applications you may already use

| App | AI feature |
|---|---|
| WhatsApp | Meta AI chat, image generation |
| Google Search | AI Overviews at the top of results |
| Google Photos | "Magic Editor", searching photos by what is in them |
| Gmail | "Help me write" |
| YouTube | Auto-captions, auto-dubbing to Telugu and Hindi |
| Canva | Magic Write, Magic Media |

## Try it

- Ask Gemini: *"How can a civil engineer in Visakhapatnam use Generative AI? Give 5 examples."* Change "civil" to your branch.
- Open [Google Translate](https://translate.google.com) and translate a paragraph from English to Telugu. Then ask Gemini to do the same. Compare.
- In WhatsApp, open Meta AI and ask it to make an image of "the Vizag lighthouse at night".

## New words

- **Application** — a use of something for a real purpose; also a software program (app).
- **Summarise** — to say the main points in fewer words.
- **Documentation** — written notes that explain how a program or product works.
- **Chatbot** — a program you can talk to by typing or speaking.
- **Voice-over** — a recorded voice that speaks over a video or slides.
- **Scheme** — a plan or program, often from the government.

# The tools: ChatGPT, Gemini, NotebookLM, AI Studio

This course uses four main tools. All of them are free to start. Make your accounts now.

## ChatGPT

**Made by:** OpenAI. **Link:** [chatgpt.com](https://chatgpt.com)

ChatGPT is the most famous AI chat tool. You type a question. It answers. You can continue the chat, and it remembers what you said earlier in the same chat.

**Good for:** writing, explaining, coding, brainstorming, images.

**How to start:** Go to the link. Sign up with your Gmail. Type in the box at the bottom. Press Enter.

**Useful features:**

- Click the **+** button to upload a file or image.
- Use the microphone icon to speak instead of typing.
- Start a **new chat** for a new topic. Old chats are saved on the left side.

## Gemini

**Made by:** Google. **Link:** [gemini.google.com](https://gemini.google.com)

Gemini is Google's AI chat tool. It works like ChatGPT. It is built into many Google products: Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides and Android phones.

**Good for:** everything ChatGPT does, plus working with Google Docs, Drive and YouTube. It is strong in Indian languages, including Telugu.

**Useful features:**

- **Gems** — you can make your own custom helper with a fixed set of instructions. For example, a "C Lab Helper" Gem.
- **Deep Research** — Gemini reads many web pages and writes a long report.
- Can look at YouTube videos and summarise them.
- Can make images and short videos.

## NotebookLM

**Made by:** Google. **Link:** [notebooklm.google.com](https://notebooklm.google.com)

NotebookLM is different. It does not answer from the internet. It answers only from the **documents you upload**. These are called **sources**. You can upload PDFs, Google Docs, websites, YouTube links and audio.

**Good for:** studying your textbooks and notes. It does not hallucinate much, because every answer points back to your source.

**Useful features:**

- Ask questions about your uploaded PDF. Every answer shows which page it came from.
- **Audio Overview** — makes a podcast where two voices discuss your document. Great for revising on the bus.
- Makes a study guide, FAQ, timeline or mind map in one click.

## Google AI Studio

**Made by:** Google. **Link:** [aistudio.google.com](https://aistudio.google.com)

Google AI Studio is for people who want to see **how the model works under the hood**. It is the developer's view of Gemini. Gemini the app is like a car. AI Studio is like the engine with the bonnet open.

**Good for:** experimenting, building a small AI app, getting an API key.

**Useful features:**

- Choose different Gemini models and compare them.
- Set a **system instruction**. This is a rule the model always follows, like "Always answer in Telugu".
- Change the **temperature**. Low = more exact. High = more creative.
- The **Build** section can create a small web app from your description.
- Get a free **API key** to use Gemini from your own Python program.

## Comparing the four

| Tool | Answers from | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| ChatGPT | Its training + web search | General chat, writing, code |
| Gemini | Its training + Google search + your Google apps | General chat, Google Docs, Indian languages |
| NotebookLM | Only your uploaded files | Study, summaries, questions about your notes |
| AI Studio | Gemini models, with your settings | Experiments, building apps, API keys |

## Other tools worth knowing

- [Claude](https://claude.ai) by Anthropic — very good for writing and coding.
- [Microsoft Copilot](https://copilot.microsoft.com) — built into Windows, Edge and Office.
- [Perplexity](https://www.perplexity.ai) — an AI search engine with sources.
- [Meta AI](https://www.meta.ai) — inside WhatsApp and Instagram.

## Try it

This is **Lab experiment 1**. Ask the same question in all four tools and compare.

```prompt
Explain how a lithium-ion battery works, for a first year engineering student. Use simple English. Give 5 bullet points.
```

- Open ChatGPT, Gemini and AI Studio. Paste the prompt. Save all three answers in a document.
- Open NotebookLM. Add a Wikipedia page about lithium-ion batteries as a source. Ask the same question.
- Which answer was the simplest? Which was the most correct? Which one showed sources?

## New words

- **Account** — your personal login for a website.
- **Chat** — a conversation; in AI tools, one conversation is saved as one chat.
- **Upload** — to send a file from your computer to a website.
- **Source** — a document that an answer comes from.
- **Custom** — made for one specific purpose.
- **System instruction** — a rule given to the AI before the chat starts.
- **Temperature** — a setting that controls how random or creative the AI answers are.
- **API key** — a secret code that lets your own program use an AI service.
- **Under the hood** — the inside workings of something (like under the bonnet of a car).

# Responsible AI

AI is powerful. Powerful things must be used with care. **Responsible AI** means using and building AI in a way that is fair, safe, honest and legal.

## Five problems to watch for

### 1. Bias

AI learns from data made by humans. Human data has unfair ideas in it. So AI can be unfair too.

Example: Ask an image tool for "a doctor". If it always shows a man, that is bias. Ask for "a software engineer". If it never shows an Indian woman, that is bias.

**What to do:** Notice it. Ask for a different output. Do not use biased output in your work.

### 2. Misinformation

AI can write false things that sound true. It can also make fake photos and fake videos (**deepfakes**). A fake video of a leader or a fake photo of a flood in Vizag can spread very fast on WhatsApp.

**What to do:** Check facts with a trusted source. Do not forward things you have not checked. Never make fake content about real people.

### 3. Privacy

Whatever you type into an AI tool may be stored by the company. It may be used to train future models.

**What to do:** Never paste passwords, Aadhaar numbers, bank details, medical records or other people's personal data into an AI tool. Use fake names in examples.

### 4. Copyright

AI models were trained on books, art and code made by people. The output may copy their style or even their exact words. Copying is a legal problem.

**What to do:** Use AI output as a draft. Add your own work. Give credit. For images and music, check the tool's licence before using them in public.

### 5. Over-dependence

If AI does all your thinking, you stop learning. In exams and interviews, there is no AI. Also, AI can be confidently wrong.

**What to do:** Use AI to learn faster, not to skip learning. Always read and understand the output. Try first, then ask AI.

## Rules for using AI in college

1. Be honest. If you used AI for an assignment, say so, if your teacher asks.
2. Check every fact and every line of code before you submit.
3. Do not put personal data of yourself or others into AI tools.
4. Do not make fake images or videos of real people.
5. Do not use AI to cheat in exams.

## Responsible AI by companies

Companies that build AI also have rules. Google, OpenAI, Microsoft and Anthropic publish **AI principles**. Common points are: be fair, be safe, be accountable, respect privacy, explain decisions, and keep a human in control.

India is also making rules. The government's **IndiaAI** mission and the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023** cover how data must be used.

## Try it

This is **Lab experiment 4**. Give these prompts to an AI tool and see what happens.

- Bias: *"Draw a picture of a nurse."* then *"Draw a picture of a CEO."* Who does it show? Try 3 times.
- Misinformation: *"Who won the 2031 cricket world cup?"* Does it make up an answer, or say it does not know?
- Privacy: Read the privacy policy of ChatGPT at [openai.com/policies/privacy-policy](https://openai.com/policies/privacy-policy). Can your chats be used for training? How do you turn it off?
- Copyright: *"Write the full lyrics of a famous Telugu film song."* Does the tool refuse? Why?
- Read [Google's AI Principles](https://ai.google/principles/) and pick the one you think is most important.

## New words

- **Responsible** — doing things in a careful, correct way; taking care of the result.
- **Ethical** — morally right; fair to everyone.
- **Bias** — an unfair leaning towards or against a group of people.
- **Misinformation** — false information, whether or not it was made on purpose.
- **Deepfake** — a fake photo, video or voice made by AI that looks real.
- **Privacy** — keeping personal information safe and private.
- **Copyright** — the legal right of a creator over their book, art, music or code.
- **Licence** — permission from the owner to use something, with conditions.
- **Accountable** — responsible for the results; someone who must answer if things go wrong.

# Writing good prompts

## What is a prompt?

A **prompt** is what you type to an AI tool. It is your question or instruction.

**Prompt engineering** is the skill of writing prompts that give you good answers. It is the most important skill in this course. A good prompt gives a good answer. A lazy prompt gives a lazy answer.

## A bad prompt and a good prompt

Bad prompt:

```prompt
write about pollution
```

Good prompt:

```prompt
You are a science teacher. Write a 150-word paragraph about air pollution in Visakhapatnam for 10th class students. Use simple English. Mention the steel plant and the port. End with 2 things students can do.
```

The second prompt tells the AI **who** it is, **what** to write, **how long**, **for whom**, **in what style** and **what to include**. That is why it works.

## The five parts of a good prompt

Remember the word **RTFCE**, or just remember these five questions.

| Part | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Role** | Who should the AI be? | "You are a C programming tutor." |
| **Task** | What should it do? | "Explain pointers." |
| **Format** | How should the answer look? | "Use 5 bullet points and one code example." |
| **Context** | What background does it need? | "I am a first year student. I know variables and loops." |
| **Example** | What does a good answer look like? | "Like this: `int *p = &x;` means p stores the address of x." |

You do not need all five every time. But the more you give, the better the answer.

## Simple tips

1. **Be specific.** "Write a notice" is weak. "Write a 100-word notice about a blood donation camp on 15 March at the GVPIHLR auditorium" is strong.
2. **Say the length.** "In 3 sentences." "Under 200 words." "A one-page report."
3. **Say the audience.** "For a 10-year-old." "For my HOD." "For a farmer."
4. **Say the format.** "As a table." "As a numbered list." "As JSON."
5. **Give an example.** Show the AI the style you want.

- Being polite does not change much. "Please" is fine, but it does not make the answer better.
- Typing in ALL CAPS does not help.
- Very long prompts with everything mixed up confuse the AI. Keep it clear.

# Types of prompts

There are a few common ways to write a prompt. Each one has a name. In the lab you will use three: **zero-shot**, **role-based** and **structured**. Let us learn them, plus two more.

We will use the same problem for all of them: *explain why the sea at RK Beach is not safe for swimming.*

## 1. Zero-shot prompt

You just ask. No examples. No role. "Zero-shot" means zero examples.

```prompt
Why is the sea at RK Beach, Visakhapatnam not safe for swimming?
```

Good for simple questions. The answer is okay but general.

## 2. Role-based prompt

You tell the AI who to be. The AI then uses the knowledge and the tone of that role.

```prompt
You are a lifeguard with 20 years of experience at RK Beach. Explain to a group of new college students why swimming here is dangerous. Speak in a friendly way.
```

The answer becomes more focused and practical. Roles you can use: teacher, doctor, lawyer, senior engineer, HR manager, tour guide, angry customer, 5-year-old child.

## 3. Structured prompt

You give the prompt a clear structure. You say exactly what sections and format you want. Many people write it with headings or labels.

```prompt
Task: Explain why swimming at RK Beach is unsafe.
Audience: First year engineering students.
Format:
1. One-line summary
2. Three reasons, as bullet points
3. A table of safe beaches near Vizag with distance from the city
4. One safety tip
Length: Under 200 words.
Language: Simple English.
```

Structured prompts give the most predictable output. Use them for reports, documents and anything you will submit.

## 4. Few-shot prompt

You give one or more **examples** of what you want. "Few-shot" means a few examples. The AI copies the pattern.

```prompt
Convert each sentence to formal English.

Casual: hey sir, can't come tomorrow, got fever
Formal: Respected Sir, I will not be able to attend tomorrow as I have a fever.

Casual: bro send the notes na
Formal:
```

Very useful for a fixed style, like translating messages or formatting data.

## 5. Chain-of-thought prompt

You ask the AI to **think step by step** before answering. This helps with maths, logic and puzzles.

```prompt
A bus leaves Vizag at 6:00 am and reaches Araku, 115 km away, at 9:30 am. It stops for 30 minutes on the way. What is its average moving speed? Think step by step, then give the final answer.
```

Without "step by step", the AI may jump to a wrong number. With it, the AI shows its working and is more often right.

## Compare them

| Type | What you give | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Zero-shot | Just the question | Quick, simple questions |
| Role-based | A role for the AI | Expert advice, a certain tone |
| Structured | Clear sections and format | Reports, documents, anything official |
| Few-shot | Examples | Fixed style or pattern |
| Chain-of-thought | "Think step by step" | Maths, logic, debugging |

You can **mix** them. A role plus a structure plus one example is a very strong prompt.

## Try it

This is **Lab experiment 5**. Pick one problem, for example: *"Should first year students buy a laptop or a tablet?"*

- Write a zero-shot prompt, a role-based prompt and a structured prompt for it.
- Run all three in the same tool. Paste the three answers side by side.
- Write 3 lines: which was best, and why.
- Try the few-shot prompt above and add 3 more casual sentences of your own.

## New words

- **Zero-shot** — a prompt with no examples.
- **Few-shot** — a prompt with a few examples.
- **Role-based** — a prompt that tells the AI who to act as.
- **Structured** — arranged in a clear order with sections or labels.
- **Chain-of-thought** — asking the AI to show its thinking step by step.
- **Tone** — the feeling of the writing: friendly, formal, strict, funny.
- **Predictable** — you can guess in advance what you will get.
- **Formal** — proper, official language, used with teachers and in letters.

# Writing and summarizing with AI

AI tools are very good at two things: **writing** text and **shortening** text. This chapter shows both.

## AI-assisted writing

The key word is **assisted**. AI helps you write. You still decide what to say. A good process has four steps.

1. **Plan.** Decide the topic, the audience and the length. Ask AI for an outline.
2. **Draft.** Ask AI to write the first version from the outline.
3. **Edit.** Read it. Fix facts. Add your own examples. Remove things you do not like. Ask AI to change the tone or the length.
4. **Check.** Read it once more. Does it sound like you? Is every fact true?

Example prompt for step 1:

```prompt
I need to write a 300-word article on "Solar power on college rooftops" for my college magazine. Give me an outline with 4 sections and one key point for each.
```

Example prompt for step 2:

```prompt
Now write the full article from this outline. Simple English, short sentences, for first year students. Mention that Visakhapatnam gets about 300 sunny days a year.
```

Example prompts for step 3:

- *"Make the second paragraph shorter."*
- *"Change the tone to be more exciting."*
- *"Add one line about cost savings in rupees."*
- *"Check the grammar and list the changes you made."*

## Other writing jobs AI does well

- **Fixing grammar:** *"Correct the grammar in this text. Do not change the meaning."*
- **Changing tone:** *"Rewrite this message to be more polite."*
- **Expanding:** *"Expand these 3 bullet points into a paragraph."*
- **Translating:** *"Translate this to Telugu."*
- **Simplifying:** *"Rewrite this for a 12-year-old."*

## Summarization

A **summary** is a short version of a long text. It keeps only the main points. AI can summarise an article, a chapter, a research paper, a meeting or a YouTube video.

Paste the text (or upload the file) and ask:

```prompt
Summarise this article in 5 bullet points. Then write a one-sentence summary. Keep the key numbers.
```

Types of summary you can ask for:

| Ask for | You get |
|---|---|
| "TL;DR in one line" | One sentence |
| "5 bullet points" | Key points |
| "Executive summary" | One short paragraph for a busy manager |
| "Summary for a 10-year-old" | Very simple version |
| "Key terms with meanings" | A glossary |
| "Questions this text answers" | Good for exam revision |

**Tip:** For long PDFs, use NotebookLM. It does not forget the start of the document, and it shows you where each point came from.

## Be careful

- A summary can miss something important. For exams, read the original once.
- AI may add things that were not in the text. Ask: *"Only use information from the text I gave."*
- Do not submit AI writing as your own creative work without editing it. Teachers can tell.

## Try it

This is **Lab experiment 6**.

- Ask ChatGPT or Gemini to write a 300-word article on *"Why every engineer should learn to swim"* (or any topic you like).
- Then ask it to summarise that same article in 3 bullet points and in one sentence.
- Try the same with a real article: copy any news article from [The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com) and summarise it.
- Paste a YouTube link into Gemini and ask for a summary of the video.

## New words

- **Assisted** — helped; AI helps you, but you are in charge.
- **Draft** — the first rough version of a piece of writing.
- **Edit** — to change and improve a piece of writing.
- **Tone** — the mood of the writing: polite, formal, exciting.
- **Summary** — a short version with only the main points.
- **TL;DR** — "too long; didn't read" — a one-line summary.
- **Executive summary** — a very short summary for a busy decision-maker.
- **Glossary** — a list of words with their meanings, like this box.

# Documents for a given context

In college and at work, you must write many formal documents. Notices, letters, reports, invitations, emails to teachers. AI can write all of these in seconds, **if you give it the context**.

## What is context?

**Context** is the background. Who is writing? To whom? Why? When? Where? What is the tone?

Without context, the AI writes a general template with blanks like [Your Name]. With context, it writes a finished document.

## The context checklist

Before you ask AI for a document, collect these:

1. **Type** of document: notice, letter, email, report, invitation, circular.
2. **From** whom: your name, roll number, class, department.
3. **To** whom: HOD, Principal, students, parents, a company.
4. **Purpose**: what is this document for?
5. **Details**: date, time, venue, names, numbers.
6. **Tone**: formal, friendly, urgent.
7. **Length**: half page, one page.

## Example 1: A notice

```prompt
Write a formal notice from the Student Council of GVPIHLR, Visakhapatnam.
Event: Blood donation camp with KGH Blood Bank.
Date: 15 March 2027, 9 am to 2 pm.
Venue: College auditorium, Madhurawada campus.
Who can join: All students and staff above 18 years.
Include: a line asking students to have breakfast before donating, and a contact (Secretary, Student Council, 98xxxxxxxx).
Format: Title, date, body, signature. Under 150 words.
```

## Example 2: An email to a teacher

```prompt
Write a short, polite email to my HOD, Dr. Rao, asking for permission to miss the lab on Friday because I am representing the college in a chess tournament in Hyderabad. My name is K. Priya, roll number 26CSE045, CSE section B. Offer to complete the lab later.
```

## Example 3: A report

```prompt
Write a one-page industrial visit report. Visit: Visakhapatnam Port, 3 February 2027. Group: 40 first year ECE students with 2 faculty. We saw: container handling, the control room, and a talk on automation. Sections: Introduction, What we saw, What we learned, Conclusion. Formal English. Third person.
```

## Example 4: An invitation

```prompt
Write an invitation card text for our department's technical fest "Tarang 2027". Date: 20 and 21 March 2027. Place: GVPIHLR campus, Visakhapatnam. Chief guest: a scientist from NSTL Visakhapatnam. Events: coding contest, robo race, paper presentation. Tone: warm and exciting. Under 80 words.
```

## Types of documents and what to remember

| Document | Key things to include |
|---|---|
| Notice | Title, date of issue, event details, who it is for, signature |
| Formal letter | Sender address, date, receiver address, subject, salutation, body, closing |
| Email | Clear subject line, short body, polite closing, your name and roll number |
| Report | Title, introduction, body with headings, conclusion, date and author |
| Invitation | Event name, date, time, place, chief guest, RSVP contact |
| Circular | Reference number, date, subject, instructions, authority |

## After AI writes it

- Read it fully. Fix any wrong details.
- Replace any [blanks] the AI left.
- Paste it into Google Docs or MS Word for formatting.
- Ask AI: *"Check this for spelling and grammar."* one last time.

## Try it

This is **Lab experiment 7**.

- Pick one: a notice, a letter, an email, a report or an invitation.
- Write down the context using the checklist above. Then write the prompt.
- Generate it. Then change one thing in the context (for example, the date) and ask AI to update only that.
- Paste it into [Google Docs](https://docs.google.com) and make it look neat. In Docs, you can also click **Help me write** to use Gemini directly.

## New words

- **Context** — the background information around a task.
- **Formal** — official and proper in style.
- **Notice** — a written announcement put up for many people to read.
- **Circular** — an official notice sent to many people in an organisation.
- **Venue** — the place where an event happens.
- **Salutation** — the greeting at the start of a letter: "Dear Sir".
- **RSVP** — a request to reply and say if you will come.
- **Third person** — writing with "the students", "they", not "I" or "we".
- **Template** — a ready-made pattern with blanks to fill in.

# Greeting cards with images and animation

In this chapter you make a greeting card. The text comes from AI. The picture comes from AI. Then you add animation in **Canva**. This is Lab experiment 8.

## Step 1: Get the text from AI

Ask ChatGPT or Gemini for the words.

```prompt
Write 3 short greeting messages for a Sankranti card for my college friends. Each under 20 words. Warm and friendly. One can mix a Telugu word.
```

Pick the one you like. Change a word or two to make it yours.

## Step 2: Get the image from AI

Many tools can make images from text. This is called **text-to-image**.

- **Gemini** — type "Create an image of ..." in the chat.
- **ChatGPT** — type "Draw ..." in the chat.
- **Canva Magic Media** — inside Canva, under Apps.
- **Microsoft Designer** — [designer.microsoft.com](https://designer.microsoft.com), free with a Microsoft account.
- **Meta AI** in WhatsApp — type "Imagine ..." in the chat.

A good image prompt describes the **subject**, the **style**, the **colours** and the **mood**.

```prompt
Create an image for a Sankranti greeting card: colourful kites flying over a village near Visakhapatnam at sunrise, a bowl of pongal in the foreground, bright festive colours, flat illustration style, no text.
```

**Tips for image prompts:**

- Say "no text". AI is bad at spelling inside images. You will add text in Canva.
- Say the style: photo, cartoon, watercolour, flat illustration, 3D.
- Say the shape if you can: square, portrait, landscape.
- Did not like it? Change one word and try again. Try 3 or 4 times.

Download the image to your computer.

## Step 3: Make the card in Canva

[Canva](https://www.canva.com) is a free online design tool. Sign up with Gmail. Students can also get Canva for Education free through the college.

Canva also has its own AI: **Magic Write** for text, **Magic Media** for images, and **Magic Design** for a full design from one line.

## Step 4: Add animation

Animation makes things move. In Canva:

1. Click on the text box. Click **Animate** at the top. Choose "Rise", "Pop" or "Typewriter".
2. Click on the image. Click **Animate**. Choose "Breathe" or "Pan".

## Step 5: Download and share

Click **Share** then **Download**. Choose:

- **MP4 Video** if you have animation. This works on WhatsApp.
- **GIF** for a short looping animation.
- **PNG** for a still image.

## Other tools for the same job

- [Adobe Express](https://www.adobe.com/express/) — similar to Canva, free plan.
- [Google Vids](https://vids.google.com) — makes short videos with AI, from Google Workspace.
- [Microsoft Designer](https://designer.microsoft.com) — makes cards and posts with AI.

## Try it

- Make a birthday card for a friend using the five steps above.
- Make a "Welcome to GVPIHLR" card for next year's students.
- Try Canva's **Magic Design**: type "Diwali greeting for a college hostel" and see what it makes in one click.
- Open [Canva Design School](https://www.canva.com/designschool/) for free short lessons.

## New words

- **Greeting** — a message of good wishes, like "Happy Sankranti".
- **Text-to-image** — making a picture from a written description.
- **Illustration** — a drawing or picture, often simple and colourful.
- **Mood** — the feeling of a picture: happy, calm, festive.
- **Landscape / portrait** — wide shape / tall shape.
- **Element** — a small design piece: an icon, shape or sticker.
- **Animation** — making things move on screen.
- **Preview** — to see how something looks before saving it.

# Generating code with AI

AI tools can write programs. You describe the problem in English. The AI writes the code in C, Python, Java or any other language. But you must **run it and check it**. This chapter shows how.

## Step 1: Describe the problem clearly

A code prompt should say:

- The **language** (C, Python, Java).
- The **input** and the **output**.
- Any **rules** (no libraries, use a loop, handle negative numbers).
- What to **include** (comments, example run).

```prompt
Write a C program that reads a number N from the user and prints whether it is a prime number. Use a simple loop. Add short comments. Handle N less than 2. Show one example input and output.
```

## Step 2: Read the code

Do not skip this. Read every line. Ask yourself: do I understand what each line does? If not, ask:

```prompt
Explain line by line what this program does. I am a first year student.
```

## Step 3: Run the code

You need a compiler or interpreter. Use any of these:

| Tool | Languages | Link |
|---|---|---|
| OnlineGDB | C, C++, Python, Java and more | [onlinegdb.com](https://www.onlinegdb.com) |
| Programiz | C, Python, Java | [programiz.com/online-compiler](https://www.programiz.com/c-programming/online-compiler/) |
| Replit | Almost all | [replit.com](https://replit.com) |
| Google Colab | Python | [colab.research.google.com](https://colab.research.google.com) |
| CodeXRay | C, with every compile stage shown | [codexray-frontend.onrender.com](https://codexray-frontend.onrender.com) |
| Your laptop | C with GCC, Python 3 | Install and use a terminal |

Paste the code. Click Run. Give the input. See the output.

## Step 4: Verify

Verify means check that the program is correct. Test it with:

- A normal input (7 → prime).
- An edge input (2 → prime, 1 → not prime, 0 → not prime).
- A big input (1000003).
- A wrong input (a letter instead of a number). What happens?

If something is wrong, go to the next chapter on debugging.

## AI tools for coding

- **ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude** — chat, paste code, ask for changes.
- **GitHub Copilot** — writes code inside your editor as you type. Free for students at [education.github.com](https://education.github.com/pack).
- **Gemini in Google Colab** — writes Python inside a notebook.
- **Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, Gemini CLI** — AI-powered editors and terminals used by professionals.
- **VS Code** — the most common editor. Copilot and Gemini plug into it.

## Good habits

1. Ask for small programs first. Then build up.
2. Ask the AI to add comments. Comments help you learn.
3. Ask: *"What are the possible bugs in this code?"* The AI often finds its own mistakes.
4. Type the code yourself at least once. Your fingers learn too.
5. Never submit code you cannot explain. In a viva, the teacher will ask.

## Try it

This is **Lab experiment 9**.

- Ask one AI tool for a program in C, Python or Java. Example problems: reverse a string, find the largest of N numbers, print a multiplication table, check a palindrome, calculate simple interest.
- Run it in [OnlineGDB](https://www.onlinegdb.com). Test with normal, edge and wrong inputs.
- Ask the AI to write the same program in a **second** language. Run that too.
- For C programs, paste the code into [CodeXRay](https://codexray-frontend.onrender.com) and see what the compiler makes from it.

## New words

- **Generate (code)** — to write code automatically.
- **Compiler** — a program that turns C or Java code into a form the computer can run.
- **Interpreter** — a program that runs Python code line by line.
- **Input / Output** — what goes into a program / what comes out.
- **Edge case** — an unusual input at the limit, like 0, 1, an empty string or a very big number.
- **Verify** — to check that something is correct.
- **Comment** — a note inside code for humans; the computer ignores it.
- **Editor** — the program where you type code, like VS Code.
- **Viva** — an oral exam where a teacher asks you questions.

# Debugging with a second AI tool

A **bug** is a mistake in a program. **Debugging** is finding and fixing it. In the lab, you will make a program with one AI tool, put bugs in it, and ask a **different** AI tool to fix it. Why a different tool? Because a second opinion catches more mistakes, just like two doctors.

## Three kinds of bugs

| Kind | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax error | The code does not compile or run at all | Missing semicolon `;` in C, wrong indentation in Python |
| Runtime error | The program crashes while running | Dividing by zero, reading outside an array |
| Logic error | The program runs but gives a wrong answer | Using `<` instead of `<=` in a loop |

Logic errors are the hardest. The computer does not complain. Only testing finds them.

## How to ask AI to debug

Give the AI **three things**: the code, the error message (or the wrong output), and what you expected.

```prompt
This C program should print the sum of numbers from 1 to N. For N = 5, it prints 10, but I expect 15. Find the bug, explain it in one line, and give the corrected code.

#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
    int n, sum = 0;
    scanf("%d", &n);
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        sum = sum + i;
    }
    printf("%d\n", sum);
    return 0;
}
```

The AI will say: the loop should be `i <= n`. That is a logic error.

For a compile error, paste the **exact** error text:

```prompt
I get this error when I compile: "error: expected ';' before 'return'". Here is the code: ...
```

## The lab process (Experiment 10)

1. **Generate.** Ask tool A (say ChatGPT) for a program. For example, a Python program to find the second largest number in a list.
2. **Run it.** Make sure it works.
3. **Break it.** Put in 2 or 3 bugs on purpose. One syntax error, one logic error. Write down what you changed.
4. **Debug.** Give the broken code to tool B (say Gemini). Do not tell it where the bugs are. Ask it to find and fix them.
5. **Compare.** Did tool B find all your bugs? Did it find something extra? Did it change anything it should not have?
6. **Run again.** Check that the fixed program works.

## Good debugging prompts

- *"Find all the bugs in this code. List each one with the line number."*
- *"Why does this give a wrong answer for input 0?"*
- *"Add print statements to help me see what the variables are doing."*
- *"Explain this error message in simple words."*
- *"Is there any input that will crash this program?"*

## Be careful

- AI sometimes "fixes" code by rewriting everything. Ask it to **change as little as possible**.
- AI may introduce a new bug while fixing the old one. Always test again.
- If the AI says the code is correct but your output is wrong, check your **input** and your **expected answer**. Sometimes the bug is in your head, not the code.

## Try it

- Do the six-step lab process with a program of your choice. Use two different tools, for example ChatGPT and Gemini, or Gemini and Claude.
- Paste a C program with a missing `;` into [OnlineGDB](https://www.onlinegdb.com). Read the compiler error. Then give the same error to an AI. Compare what each one says.
- Ask an AI: *"Give me a Python program with 3 hidden bugs for practice. Do not tell me where they are."* Then find them yourself. Then ask a second AI to check.

## New words

- **Bug** — a mistake in a program.
- **Debug** — to find and fix bugs.
- **Syntax** — the grammar rules of a programming language.
- **Runtime** — the time when a program is actually running.
- **Logic** — the reasoning or steps of a program.
- **Crash** — when a program stops suddenly because of an error.
- **Error message** — the text a compiler or program prints when something is wrong.
- **Second opinion** — asking another person (or tool) to check the same thing.

# Changing code from one language to another

Sometimes you have a program in one language and you need it in another. Maybe your lab uses C but your project uses Python. AI can **convert** (translate) code between languages in seconds. This is Lab experiment 11.

## Why convert code?

- A college lab is in C. A hackathon needs Python.
- An old program is in Java. The new app needs JavaScript for a website.
- You know Python well. You want to learn C by comparing the same program.

## How to ask

Give the full program. Say the source language and the target language. Say what must stay the same.

```prompt
Convert this C program to Python. Keep the same logic, the same input format and the same output format. Add a comment where Python does something differently from C.

#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
    int n, fact = 1;
    printf("Enter n: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) fact *= i;
    printf("Factorial = %d\n", fact);
    return 0;
}
```

The AI gives:

```
n = int(input("Enter n: "))
fact = 1
for i in range(1, n + 1):   # range stops before n + 1, so this goes 1 to n
    fact *= i
print("Factorial =", fact)
```

## Things that change between languages

| Idea | C | Python | Java |
|---|---|---|---|
| Variable | `int x = 5;` | `x = 5` | `int x = 5;` |
| Print | `printf("%d", x);` | `print(x)` | `System.out.println(x);` |
| Read input | `scanf("%d", &x);` | `x = int(input())` | `Scanner` class |
| Block | `{ ... }` | indentation | `{ ... }` |
| Integer size | fixed, can overflow | unlimited | fixed, can overflow |
| Array | `int a[5];` | `a = [0]*5` | `int[] a = new int[5];` |

Notice the last row about integers. In C, `fact` for n = 13 **overflows** (becomes a wrong number) because an `int` is only 32 bits. In Python, it does not. So the "same" program can give **different** answers. This is why you must verify.

## How to verify the converted program

1. Run the **original** program with 3 inputs. Write down the outputs.
2. Run the **converted** program with the same 3 inputs.
3. Compare. They must match.
4. Try an edge case (0, a negative number, a very big number). If the outputs differ, ask the AI why.

```prompt
The C version prints -215430144 for n = 13 but the Python version prints 6227020800. Why? Which one is correct?
```

## Good conversion prompts

- *"Convert this Python to C. Use only standard C libraries."*
- *"Convert this to Java and put it in a class called `Main` so it runs directly."*
- *"Translate this C code to Python, but write it the way an experienced Python programmer would (Pythonic style)."*
- *"Show the C and Python versions side by side in a table, line by line."*

## Try it

- Take any program from your C lab. Ask AI to convert it to Python and to Java. Run all three in [OnlineGDB](https://www.onlinegdb.com) with the same inputs.
- Take a Python program with a list. Convert it to C. See how arrays are different.
- Ask: *"Convert this program to JavaScript and make it run in a web page with a button."* Paste the result into [codepen.io](https://codepen.io) to see it work.

## New words

- **Convert / translate (code)** — to rewrite a program in a different programming language.
- **Source language** — the language the code is in now.
- **Target language** — the language you want.
- **Logic** — the steps of a program, which should stay the same after conversion.
- **Indentation** — the spaces at the start of a line; Python uses it to mark blocks.
- **Overflow** — when a number becomes too big for its storage and turns wrong.
- **Pythonic** — written in the natural style of Python.
- **Standard library** — the built-in functions that come with a language.

# Test case generation

A **test case** is one input with its expected output. We run the program with the input. If the real output matches the expected output, the test passes. If not, there is a bug.

Writing test cases is boring but very important. AI is very good at it. This is Lab experiment 12.

## Four kinds of test cases

Suppose the program is: *read a student's marks (0 to 100) and print the grade.*

| Kind | What it checks | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Normal** | Usual, everyday inputs | 72, 45, 88 |
| **Boundary** | Inputs at the edge of a range | 0, 100, 49, 50 (if 50 is pass mark) |
| **Invalid** | Inputs that should be rejected | -5, 101, "abc", empty |
| **Edge** | Strange but possible inputs | 100.5, very large number, extra spaces |

A good test set has all four kinds. Most bugs live at the **boundaries**.

## How to ask AI

Give the **problem** and the **code**. Ask for the four kinds in a table.

```prompt
Here is a problem and its solution. Generate test cases in a table with columns: Test number, Type (normal / boundary / invalid / edge), Input, Expected output, Why this test matters. Give at least 3 of each type.

Problem: Read marks (0 to 100) and print the grade: 90 and above = A, 75 to 89 = B, 50 to 74 = C, below 50 = Fail. Print "Invalid" for marks outside 0 to 100.

Code:
marks = int(input())
if marks > 100 or marks < 0:
    print("Invalid")
elif marks >= 90:
    print("A")
elif marks >= 75:
    print("B")
elif marks >= 50:
    print("C")
else:
    print("Fail")
```

The AI will give a table. Then **run each test** yourself. Some will fail. For example, the input `"abc"` will crash this program, because `int("abc")` gives an error. That is a bug the test found.

## Make a test table

| # | Type | Input | Expected | Actual | Pass? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Normal | 72 | C | C | Yes |
| 2 | Boundary | 90 | A | A | Yes |
| 3 | Boundary | 89 | B | B | Yes |
| 4 | Invalid | 101 | Invalid | Invalid | Yes |
| 5 | Invalid | abc | Invalid | crash | **No** |
| 6 | Edge | 49.9 | Fail | crash | **No** |

Fill the "Actual" column by running the program. This table is your lab record.

## Automatic tests

Professionals do not test by hand. They write **test code** that runs all the tests at once. AI can write this too.

```prompt
Write Python unit tests using pytest for the grade function above. Cover normal, boundary, invalid and edge cases.
```

For C, ask for a `main()` that calls the function with many inputs and prints PASS or FAIL for each.

## Good test prompts

- *"What inputs could break this program?"*
- *"Give 10 boundary test cases for this function."*
- *"Write a test that would catch the bug if someone changed `>=` to `>`."*
- *"My program fails test 5. Fix it without breaking the other tests."*

## Try it

- Use the grade problem above. Get test cases from AI. Run them in [OnlineGDB](https://www.onlinegdb.com) or [Programiz](https://www.programiz.com/python-programming/online-compiler/). Fill the table.
- Fix the program so that tests 5 and 6 pass. Ask the AI for help if needed.
- Take any program from Chapter 12 and generate test cases for it.
- Read a short guide: [Software testing basics – GeeksforGeeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/software-testing-basics/).

## New words

- **Test case** — one input together with the expected output.
- **Expected output** — the answer the program should give.
- **Actual output** — the answer the program really gives.
- **Pass / fail** — the test result when actual matches / does not match expected.
- **Boundary** — the edge of an allowed range, like 0 and 100.
- **Invalid** — not allowed; wrong type or out of range.
- **Unit test** — a small automatic test for one function.
- **pytest** — a popular tool for running Python tests.
- **Lab record** — the written record of your lab work.

# Slides with Gamma AI

**Gamma** is a tool that makes a full presentation from a few lines of text. You give the topic. It writes the slides, chooses a design and adds images. This is Lab experiment 13.

**Link:** [gamma.app](https://gamma.app). Sign up with Gmail. The free plan gives you credits to make several presentations.

## Step by step

1. Open Gamma. Click **Create new**.
2. Choose **Generate**. (Other options: **Paste in text** if you already have notes, or **Import file** for a Word or PDF file.)
3. Choose **Presentation**.
4. Type your topic. Be specific. Example:

```prompt
Solar energy for a college campus in Visakhapatnam: how it works, costs, benefits, a simple plan for GVPIHLR. For first year engineering students. 8 slides.
```

5. Choose the number of slides and the language. Click **Continue**.
6. Gamma shows an **outline**. Read it. Edit it. Delete or add points. Click **Continue**.
7. Choose a **theme** (colours and fonts). Click **Generate**.
8. Wait a minute. Your presentation is ready.

## Editing the slides

- Click any text to edit it.
- Click an image, then **Replace** to use another image. Gamma can also generate a new AI image from a prompt.
- Click the **+** between slides to add a slide.
- Use the right side panel for **Theme**, **Layout** and **Images**.
- Ask the AI helper (the sparkle icon) things like *"Make this slide shorter"* or *"Add a slide about costs"*.

## Exporting

Click **Share** at the top, then **Export**.

- **PowerPoint (PPTX)** — to open in MS PowerPoint or Google Slides. Needed for the lab.
- **PDF** — for printing or emailing.
- You can also **Present** directly from the browser.

## Making it good

Gamma makes a decent first draft. Make it **yours**:

- Check every fact. Gamma can hallucinate numbers.
- Replace generic images with real ones. A photo of your own campus is better than a stock image.
- Keep one idea per slide. Delete slides that say nothing new.
- The first slide should have a clear title and your name, roll number and branch.
- The last slide should be a summary or "Thank you" with a question for the audience.

## Other AI presentation tools

- [Canva Presentations](https://www.canva.com/presentations/) — Magic Design for presentations.
- [Microsoft Copilot in PowerPoint](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot) — needs a paid plan.
- [Google Slides with Gemini](https://workspace.google.com/products/slides/) — covered in the next chapter.
- [Beautiful.ai](https://www.beautiful.ai), [Tome](https://tome.app), [Pitch](https://pitch.com) — similar to Gamma.

## Try it

- Make an 8-slide presentation on an engineering topic from your branch. Examples: "How a lithium-ion battery works", "Smart traffic lights for Vizag", "3D printing in mechanical engineering", "How the Vizag port handles containers".
- Export it as PPTX. Open it in Google Slides and check that nothing broke.
- Try **Paste in text**: paste the summary you made in Chapter 9 and let Gamma turn it into slides.

## New words

- **Presentation** — a set of slides shown to an audience; also called a PPT or a deck.
- **Slide** — one page of a presentation.
- **Outline** — the list of slide titles and main points, made before the slides.
- **Theme** — the colours, fonts and style of a presentation.
- **Layout** — how text and images are arranged on a slide.
- **Export** — to save in a different file format, like PPTX or PDF.
- **PPTX** — the file format of Microsoft PowerPoint.
- **Credits** — points on a free plan; each AI generation uses some.
- **Stock image** — a general-purpose photo from an image library.

# Slides with Gemini AI

Gemini does not make a full presentation in one click like Gamma. Instead, it helps in two ways. First, it **plans** the content. Second, it works **inside Google Slides** to build it. This is Lab experiment 14.

## Way 1: Gemini plans, you build

### Step 1: Ask Gemini for the structure

```prompt
I need a 10-slide presentation on "Rainwater harvesting for apartments in Visakhapatnam" for first year civil engineering students.
For each slide give: slide title, 3 to 4 bullet points (short), and one idea for an image.
Also give speaker notes of 2 to 3 sentences for each slide.
```

Gemini writes the whole plan. Read it. Ask for changes: *"Make slide 4 about costs in rupees."* *"Add a slide with a simple diagram idea."*

### Step 2: Build the slides

Option A: **Google Slides**

1. Open [slides.google.com](https://slides.google.com). Make a new presentation.
2. Choose a theme.
3. For each slide in Gemini's plan: add a slide, paste the title and bullets.
4. Paste the speaker notes in the notes box under each slide.
5. Add images (next step).

Option B: **Gamma's "Paste in text"**. Paste Gemini's plan into Gamma. It makes the slides for you.

Option C: Ask Gemini: *"Give me this presentation as a Markdown file."* Then import it into Gamma or a tool like [Marp](https://marp.app).

### Step 3: Add images

- Ask Gemini: *"Create an image of a rooftop rainwater harvesting system on an apartment, simple diagram style."* Download and insert.
- In Google Slides, click **Insert → Image → Search the web**.
- Use [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com) or [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com) for free photos.

## Way 2: Gemini inside Google Slides

If your Google account has Gemini for Workspace (many college and some personal accounts do), there is a **Gemini button** at the top right of Google Slides.

- **Create a slide:** Click Gemini → "Create a slide about ..." It adds a slide with text and an image.
- **Create an image:** Click Gemini → "Create an image of ..." for the current slide.
- **Summarise:** Ask Gemini to summarise the deck or suggest a better title.
- **Rewrite text:** Select text and ask Gemini to make it shorter or clearer.

If you do not see the Gemini button, use Way 1. It works for everyone.

## Gamma vs Gemini

| | Gamma | Gemini |
|---|---|---|
| Makes full deck in one click | Yes | No (plans it, or slide by slide) |
| Control over content | Medium | High |
| Design | Automatic, modern | You choose in Google Slides |
| Export to PPTX | Yes | Yes, from Google Slides |
| Free | Limited credits | Yes |

**Tip:** Use both. Plan with Gemini. Build with Gamma. Polish in Google Slides.

## Try it

- Ask Gemini for a 10-slide plan on a topic from your branch. Then build it in Google Slides.
- Ask Gemini to write a **script** for what you will say on each slide. Practise it.
- Put the plan into Gamma and compare the two decks.
- Open [slides.google.com](https://slides.google.com) and look for the Gemini button. If it is there, make one slide with it.

## New words

- **Structure** — the order and parts of something.
- **Speaker notes** — notes under a slide that the presenter sees but the audience does not.
- **Deck** — another word for a full set of slides.
- **Markdown** — a simple way of writing formatted text using symbols like `#` and `-`.
- **Insert** — to add something (an image, a slide) into a document.
- **Polish** — to make the final small improvements.
- **Script** — the words you will say while presenting.
- **Workspace** — Google's set of office apps: Docs, Slides, Sheets, Gmail, Drive.

# Adding audio, video, animation and music

A presentation with only text is boring. **Multimedia** means using images, audio, video, animation and music together. This chapter shows how to add each one with AI tools. This covers Lab experiments 15 and 16.

## 1. Images

You already know this from Chapter 11. Ask Gemini, ChatGPT or Canva Magic Media for an image. Say "no text" and the style. Insert it into the slide.

For diagrams, ask: *"Draw a simple labelled diagram of a four-stroke engine, flat style, white background."*

## 2. Audio (narration)

**Narration** is a voice that explains the slide. You can record your own voice, or let AI speak.

**Record yourself:** In Canva, click **Record yourself** under Uploads. In PowerPoint, use **Insert → Audio → Record**. Your phone's voice recorder also works.

**AI voice (text-to-speech):**

- Write the script with Gemini: *"Write a 40-second narration for this slide in simple English."*
- Turn text into speech with [ElevenLabs](https://elevenlabs.io) (free plan), [Google Cloud TTS demo](https://cloud.google.com/text-to-speech) or [NaturalReader](https://www.naturalreaders.com).
- NotebookLM's **Audio Overview** can also make a two-person discussion from your notes.
- Download the MP3. Insert it into the slide.

## 3. Video

**Insert an existing video:** In Google Slides, **Insert → Video** lets you paste a YouTube link. In PowerPoint, **Insert → Video**. In Canva, drag a video from **Elements** or **Uploads**.

**Make a short AI video:**

- **Gemini** can make short video clips from a text prompt (with Veo), on supported plans.
- [Google Vids](https://vids.google.com) makes a full video from a prompt or a document.
- [Canva](https://www.canva.com) Magic Media can make short clips.
- [Pika](https://pika.art), [Runway](https://runwayml.com), [Luma](https://lumalabs.ai) — free plans with limits.

Keep videos short: 10 to 30 seconds per slide.

## 4. Animation and transitions

**Animation** moves things on one slide. A **transition** is the effect between two slides.

- **Google Slides:** Select an object → **Insert → Animation**. Choose "Fade in", "Fly in", "Appear". Set "On click" or "After previous". For transitions, **Slide → Transition**.
- **PowerPoint:** **Animations** tab and **Transitions** tab.
- **Canva:** Click an object → **Animate**. For the whole page, click the page → **Animate**.
- **Gamma:** Animations are automatic; you can turn them on or off in the theme.

Rule: use **one** transition for the whole deck. Too many effects look childish.

## 5. Background music

- Free music: [Pixabay Music](https://pixabay.com/music/), [YouTube Audio Library](https://studio.youtube.com) (under Audio Library), [Free Music Archive](https://freemusicarchive.org).
- AI-made music: [Suno](https://suno.com), [Udio](https://www.udio.com), [MusicFX by Google](https://aitestkitchen.withgoogle.com/tools/music-fx). Prompt: *"Calm instrumental background music, 1 minute, no vocals."*
- In Canva: **Elements → Audio**. Drag onto the timeline. It plays across all pages.
- In PowerPoint: insert the audio on slide 1, then tick **Play across slides** and **Loop**.
- Keep the volume low. The narration must be louder than the music.

## Putting it together (the easy way)

**Canva** is the easiest tool for all of this in one place.

1. Make the slides in Gamma or Gemini + Google Slides. Export as PPTX.
2. Open Canva → **Create a design** → **Presentation** → **Upload** the PPTX (or import from PowerPoint).
3. Add animation, narration, a video and music as above.
4. **Share → Download → MP4 Video** to get a video file. Or **Present** from Canva.

## Check the licence

Always use images, music and videos that are **free to use**. Pixabay, Pexels, Unsplash and the YouTube Audio Library are safe. Never take music from a film or a song from YouTube; that is copyright violation. AI-generated content is fine for college work, but check each tool's rules before using it commercially.

## Try it

- Take the deck you made in Chapter 16 or 17. Add one AI image, one narration (your voice or AI voice), and one short video.
- Add animations to the text on 3 slides and one transition for the whole deck.
- Add a background music track from Pixabay. Export the whole thing as an MP4 from Canva.
- Play the MP4 on your phone. Is the narration clear? Is the music too loud?

## New words

- **Multimedia** — many types of media together: text, image, audio, video.
- **Narration** — a voice that speaks over the slides.
- **Text-to-speech (TTS)** — turning written text into a spoken voice.
- **MP3** — a common audio file format.
- **Transition** — the effect when moving from one slide to the next.
- **Timeline** — the bar at the bottom of a video editor showing time.
- **Loop** — to play again and again.
- **Instrumental** — music with no singing.
- **Licence** — permission to use something; "free to use" means the licence allows it.
- **Commercial** — for business, to make money.
